extracted.intended_audience: presenters and designers of data visualizations (e.g., Keynote/PowerPoint users), and anyone producing charts/graphs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for designing truthful, legible, and information-dense quantitative graphics based on Edward Tufte's principles (graphical integrity, data-ink, chartjunk, data density, small multiples, sparklines, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical integrity — proportional representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of numbers, as physically measured on the surface of the graph itself, should be directly proportional to the numerical quantities represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scaling or graphical encodings that distort the true magnitude of numerical changes (see Lie Factor example where a 53% numerical change is shown as 783%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical integrity — clear, detailed, thorough labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, detailed and thorough labeling should be used to defeat graphical distortion and ambiguity. Write out explanations of the data on the graph itself. Label important events in the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include axis labels, units, annotations for key events, and direct text explanations on the graphic rather than relying solely on captions or legends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical integrity — show data variation, not design variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Show data variation, not design variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices should not create apparent changes that are artifacts of styling; visual differences should reflect actual data differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical integrity — use deflated/standardized units for monetary time-series
rubrics_metrics.description: In time-series displays of money, deflated and standardized units of monetary measurement are nearly always better than nominal units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust monetary series for inflation or otherwise standardize units to avoid misleading trends produced by nominal values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical integrity — limit information-carrying dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of information carrying (variable) dimensions depicted should not exceed the number of dimensions in the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inventing extra visual dimensions that imply multivariate structure not present in the data; keep encoding faithful to underlying variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical integrity — do not quote data out of context
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphics must not quote data out of context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide necessary context (time period, population, units, baseline) so readers interpret values correctly and not as isolated or misleading points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lie Factor (metric for graphical distortion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lie Factor = (size of effect shown in the graphic) / (size of effect in the data). If the Lie Factor is greater than 1 the graph overstates the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate Lie Factor to diagnose over- or under-statement. Tufte gives an example where a 53% numerical change is represented by a 783% graphical change (Lie Factor ≈ 14.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-Ink (concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data Ink is the ink on a graph that represents data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which marks in a graphic carry data-information versus decorative or redundant marks; strive to maximize the former.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-ink ratio (metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The data-ink ratio is calculated by 1 minus the proportion of the graph that can be erased without loss of data-information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher data-ink ratio indicates less non-informative ink; aim to remove non-essential ink elements to increase the ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-Ink principle — above all else show data
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all else show data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize presenting the data itself rather than emphasizing decoration, branding, or gratuitous graphical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-Ink principle — maximize the data-ink ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximize the data-ink ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design charts so that most of the ink on the page encodes information; reduce gridlines, heavy borders, and extraneous shading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-Ink principle — erase non-data-ink
rubrics_metrics.description: Erase non-data-ink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove purely decorative elements (background images, heavy ornamentation) that do not convey data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-Ink principle — erase redundant data-ink
rubrics_metrics.description: Erase redundant data-ink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid duplicating the same information in multiple visual forms (e.g., over-annotated tick marks or repeated labels) when one clear encoding suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-Ink principle — revise and edit
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise and edit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively strip away non-essential elements; test whether removing ink harms comprehension and keep the graphic as lean as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chartjunk — avoid excessive decorative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Chartjunk is the excessive and unnecessary use of graphical effects in graphs (e.g., moiré vibration, heavy grids, self-promoting graphics used to show a designer's skill rather than the data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use decorative effects that distract from data; examples of chartjunk include gratuitous 3-D effects, patterned fills that obscure values, and heavy visual textures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data density — favor high data density
rubrics_metrics.description: The data density of a graph is the proportion of the total size of the graph that is dedicated to displaying data. Tufte prefers high data density graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximize the amount of data shown per unit area where legible; use compact displays rather than sparse charts that waste space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shrink Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Many graphs can be shrunk way down without losing legibility or information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce scale and whitespace where possible to increase data density and fit more information into the visual field; ensure readability remains acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small multiples
rubrics_metrics.description: Small multiples are a series of the same small graph repeated in one visual; they are a great tool to visualize large quantities of data and many dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small multiples to compare related series or to show many facets of the same measure while keeping consistent scales and encodings across panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spark-lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Sparklines are data-intense, design-simple, word-sized graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparklines to show trends or movements (e.g., stock movements) inline with text or in compact small-multiple arrangements; keep them minimal and contextually labeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and anti-patterns (illustrative guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tufte demonstrates many before-and-after examples: low graphical integrity graphs (high Lie Factor), electroencephalogram with data-ink ratio 1, and charts considered the 'worst' due to chartjunk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study concrete examples of misleading or cluttered charts and their cleaned, high-integrity redesigns to learn practical editing choices.
